body:
A Faith and an Empire Spread (lesson): Reasons Arabic spread: it was the language of the Quran, so it grew as more people became Muslim; the caliphs used it for government across a huge area; merchants and pilgrims used it as a common language. A shared language and shared law for contracts let a merchant travel from Cordoba to Cairo to Baghdad and trade with people he had never met; the hajj also brought people, goods and news together.

The House of Wisdom (assignment):
Sourcing 1. Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, in Baghdad in the early 800s, dedicated to the caliph al-Ma'mun (ruled 813-833).
Sourcing 2. Authors depended on rulers for support, so praise may be partly flattery; but it also shows that the ruler was known for supporting scholars.
Context 1. Baghdad was a huge, wealthy trading capital; paper was now available; the caliphs paid scholars to collect and translate Greek, Persian, Syriac and Sanskrit works.
Context 2. People inherited and divided property, went to court, traded, measured land and built canals, so they needed practical mathematics; it was a complex, commercial, farming society.
Claim. Model: Rulers and scholars invested in books because knowledge was useful and brought prestige. Al-Khwarizmi says his book covers what "people constantly need" in "inheritance ... trade ... measuring land, digging canals," and he credits al-Ma'mun's "love of learning" and help to scholars. The secondary reading shows rulers paid for translation from many languages.

Ideas That Traveled On (assignment): Hindu-Arabic numerals and zero: from India; adopted and spread by scholars such as al-Khwarizmi; reached Europe through Spain and North Africa, later replacing Roman numerals; both continuity and change. Algebra: built on older Greek, Babylonian and Indian methods but organized as a new subject by al-Khwarizmi (mostly change); translated into Latin in the 1100s. Paper: from China, reached Baghdad by the late 700s, spread to Egypt, Spain and Europe; made books cheaper (continuity of the technique, change in its use). Canon of Medicine: Ibn Sina combined Greek medicine with his own observations; translated into Latin and used in European universities for centuries.

Baghdad's Golden Age (assessment): Either claim can earn full credit. Trade evidence: Baghdad's location on the Tigris and its trade links; wealth that paid for scholars; paper-making learned through contact with China; a shared language of trade. Scholarship evidence: caliphs such as al-Ma'mun paid for translation; scholars of many faiths; new work by al-Khwarizmi and Ibn Sina. A strong answer weighs the causes ("without trade wealth there would be no money for scholars, but wealthy trading cities did not all become centers of learning").

Scoring tip: for the House of Wisdom, Advanced work notices that the preface is both evidence of the caliph's support and a piece of flattery, and uses al-Khwarizmi's list of everyday uses to explain why rulers valued the work. For Ideas That Traveled On, accept small differences in dates if the order of events is right.
